Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title. What will you get? Tick one.   a story    rules    ideas

What Keeps a Friendship Alive?

A magazine article · about 430 words · B2+ · written for this book

AThink of the person who would answer your call at three o’clock in the morning. Most people can name one or two such friends, not twenty. Social media may show us hundreds of “friends”, but the people who really stand by us are rare. So what turns a classmate into a friend for life?

BMore than two thousand years ago, the Greek philosopher Aristotle described three kinds of friendship. The first is friendship of usefulness, which exists because two people help each other, like classmates who share lecture notes. The second is friendship of pleasure, where people simply enjoy the same things, such as football or music. The third kind, which Aristotle valued most, is friendship of character: two people like each other for who they are. In his view, only this kind truly lasts.

CTrust is the foundation that every close friendship stands on. A friend who keeps your secrets and tells you the truth, even when it hurts, is worth more than ten who only say nice things. Trust grows slowly, through small actions: arriving on time, returning a borrowed book, remembering the date of an important exam. However, a single moment of betrayal can destroy it.

DFriendship also needs time, which is something many young people feel they do not have. Between lectures, part-time jobs and family duties, it is easy to drift apart from people we love. Friends who stay close usually find small ways to keep in touch: a voice message, a shared joke, a cup of tea after classes. Distance is another test: when a friend moves to another city or country, the friendship survives only if both people make an effort.

EIn Uzbekistan, friendship has its own traditions. Many groups of old friends meet regularly at a gap, a gathering where they take turns hosting one another, at home or in a çoyxona. Some groups keep this habit for decades, from their school days until they are grandparents. Such meetings show that friendship is not only a feeling but also a habit that people practise.

FFriends do not have to be identical. In fact, a friend who sees the world differently can help us grow. Dilnoza, a student whose best friend studies medicine, says that their friendly arguments have taught her more than many lectures. What matters is mutual respect, not the same opinions.

GPerhaps the secret of a lasting friendship is simple: it is a relationship in which both people give more than they take. So choose friends who make you better — and be the kind of friend that you would like to have.

Which paragraph is the introduction (the gate)? Which is the conclusion (the roof)?
Jigsaw option. Group A: paragraphs A–C · Group B: D–E · Group C: F–G. Become experts on your part, then teach it to a new mixed group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which paragraph describes friendship in your own life best? Which idea do you disagree with? Why?

Language toolkit: relative clauses

10 MIN

Relative clauses add information about a noun without starting a new sentence.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (A) Think of the person would answer your call at three o’clock in the morning.

2. (B) The first is friendship of usefulness, exists because two people help each other …

3. (B) The second is friendship of pleasure, people simply enjoy the same things …

4. (C) Trust is the foundation every close friendship stands on.

5. (E) … a gap, a gathering they take turns hosting one another …

6. (F) Dilnoza, a student best friend studies medicine, …

Who goes where? rule
WordUse it forExample from the article
whopeopleA friend who keeps your secrets …
whichthings, ideas… friendship of usefulness, which exists because …
thatpeople or thingsthe foundation that every close friendship stands on
whereplaces and situationsa gathering where they take turns hosting
whosebelonging (= his / her)a student whose best friend studies medicine

Three rules

  • One subject only: a friend who keeps secrets ✓  ·  a friend who he keeps secrets ✗
  • Commas? Use who / which, never that: Aristotle, who lived in Greece, … ✓  ·  Aristotle, that … ✗
  • Where already means “in it”: the çoyxona where we meet ✓  ·  where we meet there ✗
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. I have a friend which lives in Samarkand.
2. This is the çoyxona where we meet there.
3. Jasur, that studies law, is my oldest friend.
4. A friend who he tells lies is not a real friend.
5. The book what you gave me was about friendship.
6. Aziz is the friend whose his sister studies with me.
7. Samarkand is the city which I met my best friend.
8. The classmates which I study with are very reliable.

Level up: signposts and reference

CONTINUED

Signposts show where the essay is going. Reference words point back to an idea, so you do not repeat the same noun.

ToolPhrasesExample
Signposting
shows the next step		The first / A further / A final quality is … · Beyond …, …Beyond loyalty, a good friend needs the courage to be honest.
Reference words
this / such + noun		this quality · such friendships · this habit · the former … the latterSuch friendships rarely survive without regular contact.
Nominalisation
verb / adjective → noun		loyal → loyalty · grow → growth · lose touch → loss of contactFriends help each other grow. → Personal growth is the deepest gift of friendship.
Reduced relatives
drop who is / which are		a friend (who is) willing to listen · notes (which are) shared by classmatesA friend living abroad needs more effort to stay close.

The Blueprint: build it like a hovli

10 MIN

An essay is a group of paragraphs that answer one question. Every essay you write this year stands on three parts: introduction, body, conclusion.

The reader moves the same way: through the darvoza, into each room, then under the ayvon roof.

Part of the hovliPart of the essayWhat goes insideWords
The darvozaIntroductionHook → background → thesis (main idea + 3 points)≈ 50
Rooms 1, 2, 3Body paragraphsOne point per room: door = topic sentence, furniture = support + example, window = concluding sentence≈ 60 × 3
Stepping stonesLinking wordsFirstly · Secondly · Finally · To sum up—
The ayvon roofConclusionThesis in new words + summary + final thought. No new points.≈ 40
Compare it think
Paragraph · Stop 2Essay · Stop 7Opinion essay · Stop 8
Goalone main ideaanswer one question in 3 pointswin the reader to ONE side
Main ideatopic sentencethesis (end of the introduction)thesis = opinion + reasons
Buildingone roomhovli: gate, three rooms, ayvonmadrasa: gate, minarets, dome

Walk through the hovli

CONTINUED
Task: What makes a good friend? Write an essay of 250–300 words.
The darvoza
HOOKAn old Uzbek proverb says that it is better to have a hundred friends than a hundred som. BACKGROUNDToday, however, many of us have hundreds of online contacts but are not sure which of them are real friends. THESISIn my view, a good friend is someone who is loyal, who is honest even when it is difficult, and who helps us to grow.
Room 1
(1) Firstly, a good friend is loyal. (2) Loyalty means standing by someone not only at weddings and birthdays but also in difficult times. (3) For example, when Jasur’s family moved to a new mahalla, his school friend Bekzod spent the whole weekend helping them carry furniture and never mentioned it again. (4) A friend who disappears when life becomes hard was never really a friend.
Room 2
Secondly, a good friend is honest. It is easy to praise someone, but it takes courage to point out a mistake. A real friend will tell you, kindly but clearly, that your plan is risky or that your essay needs another draft. Honest advice, which may hurt for a moment, often saves us from much bigger problems later.
Room 3
Finally, good friends help each other to grow. People who spend a lot of time together often share habits, so a hard-working friend can make us more ambitious. For instance, two classmates who prepare for exams together can push each other to aim higher. In this way, friendship becomes a school where both people learn.
The ayvon roof
To sum up, good friends are loyal and honest, and they help us to become better people. Such friends are rare, which is why we should value them. If you want to find a good friend, start by becoming one.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Practise them on two paragraphs first, then use them on your own essay.

CriterionA C1 essay …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear thesis from the darvoza to the ayvon roof
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (door · furniture · window) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: relative clauses (who, which, that, where, whose)

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Two students wrote Room 1 for the model-essay task (What makes a good friend?). Mark both.

Student A
Firstly, good friend is very very important for the life. A good friend is loyal and stays with you in difficult times. My friend who he lives in Samarkand always help me. For example, he helped to me when I was ill: he brought me his lecture notes every day for two weeks. We are friends since the first class. In conclusion, I want to say that the friend must to be loyal.
Student B
The first quality of a good friend is loyalty. Loyalty means standing by someone not only in moments of celebration but also when life becomes difficult. A case in point is a classmate who visits you in hospital every day, long after the get-well messages have stopped. Such loyalty cannot be bought; it is earned slowly, through small acts of support that are rarely mentioned again.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title. Is the writer for zoos, against zoos, or both? Tick one.
for    against    both sides

Zoos: Prisons or Protectors?

A magazine article · about 390 words · B2+ · written for this book

AEvery year, millions of people around the world visit zoos. For many children, a trip to the zoo is the first chance to see a lion, a giraffe or an elephant with their own eyes. However, behind the excitement there is a serious question: is it right to keep wild animals in captivity?

BIt is often argued that modern zoos are no longer simply places of entertainment. Many of them take part in conservation programmes which protect endangered species. By breeding animals in captivity, zoos have helped to save some species from extinction, and several animals that had disappeared from the wild have later been released into their natural habitats. The Arabian oryx and Przewalski’s horse are two well-known examples.

CSupporters also believe that zoos play an important educational role. Seeing a living animal can make a much stronger impression than reading about it in a book or watching a documentary. Many zoos organise lessons for schoolchildren and help to train young scientists. Therefore, it could be said that zoos help to raise awareness of wildlife among young people.

DCritics, however, believe that no zoo can replace the wild. Even in a large enclosure, an animal cannot hunt, travel long distances or live in a natural social group. Animals such as elephants and polar bears, which cover great distances in nature, may suffer most. Some captive animals walk in circles or repeat the same movement again and again, which scientists see as a sign of stress. For this reason, some people even call zoos cruel.

EOpponents also point out that the money spent on zoos might be used more effectively elsewhere. Instead of building enclosures, they suggest, governments should create national parks and wildlife sanctuaries, where animals can live freely while scientists still study and protect them.

FIn Uzbekistan, this debate has a local dimension. The Jeyran Ecocentre in the Bukhara region, for instance, breeds rare animals such as the goitered gazelle in large semi-wild areas. Centres like this show that there may be a middle way between a traditional zoo and complete freedom.

GPerhaps the real question is not whether zoos should exist, but what kind of zoos society should accept. If zoos want to survive in the 21st century, they must put animal welfare first. Only then can they become true protectors rather than prisons.

The writer never says “I think”. Can you still find their opinion?
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–C, Group B on D–E, Group C on F–G. Read your part, agree on its main idea, then form new mixed groups and teach it in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which argument in the article is the strongest? Which is the weakest? Why?

Language toolkit: modal verbs

10 MIN

Modal verbs work like a volume control: they show how sure you are and how strongly you want something to happen.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (E) … governments create national parks and wildlife sanctuaries …

2. (D) Animals such as elephants and polar bears … suffer most.

3. (E) … the money spent on zoos be used more effectively elsewhere.

4. (C) … it be said that zoos help to raise awareness of wildlife …

5. (G) If zoos want to survive in the 21st century, they put animal welfare first.

6. (B) often argued that modern zoos are no longer simply places of entertainment.

The volume control rule
VolumeUseExample from the article
🔊 strong necessitymustZoos must put animal welfare first.
🔉 adviceshould / ought toGovernments should create national parks.
🔈 possibilitymay / might / couldElephants may suffer most.
📣 a general viewIt is often argued that … / It could be said that …It is often argued that zoos protect species.

Three rules

  • Modal + base verb: should create ✓  ·  should to create ✗
  • No -s after he / she / it: it must put ✓  ·  it musts put ✗
  • Passive: modal + be + past participle → Animals must be protected.
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Zoos should to protect endangered species.
2. A zoo musts give animals enough space.
3. Wild animals should not keep in small cages.
4. Breeding programmes can to save rare animals.
5. It often argued that zoos are cruel.
6. Zoos ought protect endangered animals.
7. Rare birds must be protect from hunters.
8. Visitors don’t must feed the animals.

Level up: hedging and concession

CONTINUED

At C1 you show how sure you are, and you admit what is true on the other side before you answer it.

ToolPhrasesExample
Hedging
makes a claim less absolute		arguably · tend to · it would appear that · there is little evidence thatLarge animals tend to suffer most in small enclosures.
Concession
admits a point, then answers it		Admittedly, … ; nevertheless, … · While it is true that …, … · Granted, …While it is true that enclosures limit movement, modern zoos have made them far larger.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		protect → protection · lose → loss · aware → awarenessZoos protect species. → The protection of species is the strongest argument for zoos.
Stance adverbs
show your attitude in one word		undeniably · understandably · surprisingly · cruciallyUnderstandably, many visitors feel uncomfortable near a lonely elephant.

B2 sentenceC1 sentence

Do not over-hedge

✗ It could perhaps possibly be argued that zoos may sometimes be slightly useful.
✓ Zoos are arguably useful for conservation.  — one hedge per claim is enough.

Walk through the madrasa

CONTINUED
Task: Zoos should be closed because keeping wild animals in captivity is cruel. To what extent do you agree?
The gate
HOOKFew experiences excite a child more than seeing a real tiger for the first time. BACKGROUNDHowever, in recent years, many people have started to question whether it is fair to keep wild animals behind fences. THESISIn my opinion, zoos should not be closed, because they protect endangered species and teach people to respect wildlife.
Minaret 1
(1) Firstly, modern zoos play a key role in conservation. (2) When a species is close to extinction, breeding it in captivity may be the only way to save it. (3) For example, the Arabian oryx survived thanks to breeding programmes and was later released into the wild. (4) Without such programmes, many more species could disappear forever.
Minaret 2
Secondly, zoos raise awareness of wildlife among ordinary people. A documentary can show an elephant, but only a real visit lets a child see its size and hear its voice. Many zoos also run lessons for schoolchildren, which encourage young people to care about nature. As a result, zoos help to create future protectors of the environment.
Guarded gate
Some people argue that life in an enclosure is cruel, since animals cannot move freely or hunt. Although this is a serious problem in poorly managed zoos, it is a reason to improve them, not to close them. Larger enclosures and strict welfare rules can make captivity much less stressful.
The dome
To sum up, I firmly believe that zoos deserve a place in modern society. They save endangered animals and teach visitors to value wildlife. However, governments must make sure that every zoo puts animal welfare first.

Be the examiner

7 MIN

Examiners use four criteria. Practise them on two paragraphs first, then use them on your own essay.

CriterionA C1 essay …
T · Taskanswers the exact question and keeps one clear position from the gate to the dome
O · Organisationhas one idea per paragraph (R.E.A.L.) and links ideas with more than Firstly / Secondly
V · Vocabularyuses precise topic words and collocations in an academic tone
G · Grammaruses a range of structures with few errors; in this stop: modal verbs (must / should / may + base verb) and hedging

Score each criterion: 1 = not yet · 2 = almost · 3 = yes

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title. Is the writer for phones, against them, or both? Tick one.
for    against    both sides

Phones in Class: Tool or Trap?

A magazine article · about 450 words · B2+ · written for this book

AWalk into almost any lecture hall today and you will see the same picture: rows of students, each with a glowing screen in front of them. For some teachers, this is a sign of progress. For others, it is the biggest threat to learning since the excuse “the dog ate my homework”. So should smartphones have a place in the classroom, or should they stay in students’ bags?

BSupporters point out that a smartphone is a library, a dictionary and a calculator in one pocket. When a student meets an unfamiliar word, they can check it in seconds, whereas their parents had to find a heavy paper dictionary. Online quizzes, educational apps and shared documents can also make lessons more interactive, especially in large groups where not everyone gets a chance to speak.

CAnother argument for phones is that young people need to learn to use technology responsibly. Although phones can be a distraction, banning them does not teach students how to manage them. Some educators believe that schools should teach digital literacy instead: how to check whether a website is reliable, how to protect their data and how to switch off notifications when it is time to work.

DOn the other hand, critics argue that phones undermine concentration. A single notification can pull a student out of a difficult task, and it can take a while to regain focus. Despite good intentions, many students who open their phone “just to check one word” find themselves scrolling through social media ten minutes later. Many popular apps are designed to hold our attention for as long as possible, so the battle is hardly a fair one.

EOpponents also worry about fairness and safety. Not every family can afford an expensive phone, and lessons built around apps may leave some students behind. Phones can also bring cyberbullying into the classroom: a photo taken during a lesson can be shared with hundreds of people before the bell rings. For these reasons, a number of countries have introduced rules that restrict phone use in schools.

FIn Uzbekistan, the question is just as real. In many universities, teachers share homework and materials through Telegram groups, so students need their phones to study. In spite of this, the same teachers often ask students to keep their phones face down during lectures. The phone, it seems, is both a helper and a rival.

GPerhaps the answer lies not in a total ban or total freedom, but in clear rules. Phones could be used when a task requires them and put away when it does not. A ban is easy to announce; however, responsible use takes time to learn. It may also be the only skill that lasts beyond the classroom.

Count the arguments on each side. Is the writer really fair?
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–C, Group B on D–E, Group C on F–G. Agree on the main idea, then teach it to a new mixed group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Is the article really balanced? Which argument is the strongest? Why?

Language toolkit: contrast linkers

Contrast linkers connect the two wings. They show the reader that the other side follows.

Notice find it

Four doors, four grammars rule
LinkerWhat comes after itExample from the article
However, / On the other hand,new sentence + commaOn the other hand, critics argue …
although / even thoughsubject + verbAlthough phones can be a distraction, …
whereas / whilesubject + verb… in seconds, whereas their parents had …
despite / in spite ofnoun or -ing, no verbDespite good intentions, many students …

Three rules

  • One door is enough: Although phones help, they distract. ✓  ·  Although …, but … ✗
  • Despite + noun / -ing: despite the ban ✓ · despite being useful ✓  ·  despite of ✗
  • However after a full stop (or ;): Phones help. However, they distract. ✓

verb or adjective → noun		ban → the introduction of a ban · use responsibly → responsible useSchools ban phones. → The introduction of a ban does little to build self-control.

5

Walk through the caravanserai

CONTINUED
Task: Discuss the arguments for and against allowing students to use smartphones in university lectures.
The gate
HOOKNot long ago, a phone ringing during a lecture was a small scandal. BACKGROUNDToday, almost every student carries a powerful computer in their pocket, and universities must decide what to do with it. THESISThis essay will examine the main arguments for and against allowing smartphones in lectures.
Left wing
room 1
(1) On the one hand, smartphones give students instant access to information. (2) When a lecturer mentions an unfamiliar term, students can look it up immediately instead of waiting until they get home. (3) For example, a student in a history lecture can check a date or a map without interrupting the class. (4) In this way, the phone becomes a pocket library.
Left wing
room 2
Moreover, phones can make large lectures more interactive. In a hall of a hundred students, only a few usually have the chance to speak. However, a quick online poll allows everyone to answer at the same time, and the lecturer can see at once who has understood. As a result, even quiet students take part.
Right wing
room 3
On the other hand, phones are a constant source of distraction. Although many students open their phone with good intentions, a single notification can pull them away from the lecture. For instance, a student who wants to check one word may end up reading messages for ten minutes. Clearly, this undermines concentration.
Right wing
room 4
Another argument against phones is that they can harm students’ well-being. Despite clear rules, photos taken in class can be shared online without permission, which may lead to cyberbullying. Even a harmless joke can hurt when hundreds of people see it. For this reason, some lecturers prefer a phone-free room.
The well
To sum up, smartphones can enhance learning, whereas careless use can undermine it. On balance, a total ban does not seem to be the answer; universities should rather set clear rules and teach students to use their phones responsibly.

1. Underline the thesis. Does the gate give an opinion?

yes    no — it is neutral

2. Room 1: write R, E, A or L for each sentence.

3. The courtyard: which phrase takes the reader from the left wing to the right wing?

4. Count the rooms. Why must the wings be equal?

FOR    AGAINST

5. The view at the well is …

strong    cautious    missing

Which words show it?

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title. What will the writer do with city life? Tick one.
praise it    attack it    weigh it

City Life on the Scales

A magazine article · about 420 words · B2+ · written for this book

AEvery summer, young people from small towns and villages across Uzbekistan pack a suitcase and head for the big city. Some go to study, others to find work, and many never come back. For their grandparents, this choice can be hard to understand. Is city life really better than village life, or is it just louder?

BThe most obvious advantage of the city is opportunity. Big cities such as Tashkent offer far more jobs, universities and training courses than small towns do. A graduate who dreams of a career in IT, banking or medicine will usually find a much wider choice in the capital than in a rural district, and salaries there are often higher, too.

CCity life is also more convenient in many ways. Hospitals are better equipped, shops stay open later, and buses and the metro connect most districts of Tashkent. For students, the city is probably the best place to meet people from different regions and backgrounds, which can make their view of the world broader.

DHowever, city life has a price — quite literally. The cost of living in the capital is a lot higher than in the countryside, and rent alone can take a large part of a young person’s salary. Traffic congestion makes the daily commute longer and more stressful, and the air in busy streets is not as clean as the air in the mountains.

EMany people also feel that the city is lonelier than the village. In a traditional mahalla or a village, neighbours know each other, help at weddings and look after each other’s children. In a large block of flats, by contrast, people may live next door for years without learning each other’s names. Life moves faster, and there is less time for family and friends.

FVillage life, of course, has its own weights on the scales. Houses are usually cheaper and bigger, many families grow their own fruit and vegetables, and the pace of life is slower. On the other hand, young people in rural areas often have fewer chances to study or find well-paid work, and a specialist doctor may be hours away.

GSo which pan of the scales is heavier? The answer depends on who is standing at the bazaar. For an ambitious graduate, the city may be the best choice; for a young family that wants space and calm, the village may be just as attractive. Perhaps the happiest people are those who take the best of both: a career in the city and long summers at their grandmother’s house.

Count the weights in each pan. Which side gets more?
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–C, Group B on D–E, Group C on F–G. Agree on the main idea, then teach it to a new mixed group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Which pan is heavier in this article? Do you agree with the needle in paragraph G? Why?

PatternRuleExample from the article

The Blueprint: the bazaar scales

10 MIN

An advantages–disadvantages essay puts one thing on the scales — a place, an idea, a change — and weighs its good and bad sides. Typical tasks: What are the advantages and disadvantages of …? · Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?

Every point needs a weight, a concrete example. The needle, the conclusion, says which pan is heavier.

The needleConclusionSum up both pans → which side is heavier, and for whom≈ 50

Weigh the model essay

CONTINUED
Task: What are the advantages and disadvantages of living in a big city?
The stand
HOOKBright lights, fast buses and a café on every corner: for many young people, the big city is a dream. BACKGROUNDEvery summer, graduates from small towns pack their bags and head for the capital. THESISHowever, life in a big city has both clear advantages and serious disadvantages.
Left pan
TOPICOn the positive side, a big city offers far more opportunities than a small town. (1) First of all, the choice of jobs and universities is much wider. WEIGHTFor example, a graduate who dreams of a career in IT will find many more companies in the capital than in a rural district. (2) Moreover, everyday life is more convenient, as hospitals are better equipped and shops stay open later. WEIGHTEven a student without a car can reach most parts of the city by bus or metro.
Right pan
TOPICOn the negative side, city life can be expensive and stressful. (1) The cost of living is a lot higher than in the countryside. WEIGHTFor instance, the rent for a small flat can take a large part of a young worker’s salary. (2) In addition, the city is often noisier, more crowded and lonelier than a village. WEIGHTNeighbours in a block of flats may never learn each other’s names, whereas in a village everyone knows everyone.
The needle
To sum up, the city offers more opportunities, but it also asks for more money and more patience. On balance, the advantages seem heavier for young people at the start of their careers, although the village may still be the better choice for those who value calm and community.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title. What will the article mostly do? Tick one.
describe a problem only   blame someone for it   describe a problem and suggest solutions

A Way Out of Plastic

A magazine article · about 420 words · B2+ · written for this book

AWalk through any bazaar in Uzbekistan on a Saturday morning and count the plastic bags. A kilo of tomatoes goes into one bag, the herbs into another and the bread into a third. Each bag is used for perhaps twenty minutes, but it may stay in the environment for hundreds of years. Multiply this by every shopper in every town, and the size of the problem becomes clear.

BPlastic pollution matters because plastic does not stay where we drop it. Wind carries bags into fields and rivers, where animals can mistake them for food. Over time, large pieces break into tiny particles called microplastics, which scientists have found in water, in soil and even in food. Litter also blocks drains and canals, so streets flood more easily after heavy rain.

CThe most direct solution is to make single-use plastic less attractive. Many countries have already introduced bans or small charges on plastic bags. If shops charge even a small amount for each bag, many customers will bring their own. The idea is simple: when something is free, people waste it; when it has a price, they think twice.

DA second solution is to turn rubbish into a resource. In several European countries, shoppers pay a small deposit on every bottle and get the money back when they return it. Because an empty bottle now has value, fewer bottles end up as litter. If every family in our country sorted its waste and returned its bottles, our landfills would grow far more slowly.

ELaws and money are not enough, however; habits must change too. Schools and the media can raise awareness by showing young people where their rubbish really goes. Here, Uzbekistan has a powerful tradition to build on: the haşar, when neighbours in a mahalla work together to clean streets and plant trees. If a mahalla organised a regular haşar against plastic, children would learn that a clean street is a shared responsibility.

FOf course, each solution has its limits. Bans can be ignored if nobody checks them, and recycling needs factories, collection points and trained workers. Awareness campaigns work slowly. For this reason, a mix of several measures is likely to work better than any single one.

GThe plastic bag at the bazaar looks like a small thing, but small things add up. Governments can make the rules, businesses can offer alternatives, and each of us can carry a cloth bag. If we act together now, the next generation will inherit cleaner rivers. If we wait, the problem will only grow.

Find the bridge: where does the problem end and the solutions begin?
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–B (the problem), Group B on C–D (two solutions), Group C on E–F (one more solution and the limits). Read your part, agree on its main idea, then form mixed groups and teach it in 60 seconds. Read G together.
Talk after reading: Which solution would work best in your town or village? Which would be the hardest? Why?

Real or imagined? rule
TypeFormUse it for …Example from the article
ZeroIf / When + present, presentalways trueWhen it is free, people waste it.
FirstIf + present simple, will + verba real, likely planIf shops charge for bags, people will bring their own.
SecondIf + past simple, would + verba “dream” planIf every family sorted waste, landfills would grow slowly.

Three rules

  • No will in the if-part: If shops charge ✓  ·  If shops will charge ✗
  • Second: past form, present meaning: If every family sorted … (now). Formal: If I were …
  • Comma: if-part first → comma. If-part second → no comma: Rivers would be cleaner if …

5

Model essay

CONTINUED
Task: Plastic waste is a growing problem in many towns in Uzbekistan. What can be done to reduce it?
Left bank
HOOKA plastic bag is used for minutes, but it can outlive the person who carried it. PROBLEMIn many towns, single-use bags and bottles now fill streets, canals and landfills. WHY IT MATTERSThis litter spoils public spaces, harms animals and slowly turns into microplastics. THESISHowever, the problem can be tackled if we put a price on plastic and make clean streets everyone’s business.
Pillar 1
(1) The first solution is to make single-use plastic cost something. (2) If shops charged a small fee for every bag and bottles carried a refundable deposit, customers would think twice before throwing plastic away. (3) For instance, in several European countries, shoppers get money back for every empty bottle they return, so bottles are collected instead of dropped. (4) As a result, far less plastic would reach our streets and landfills.
Pillar 2
The second solution is to make clean streets a shared responsibility. Schools could teach children to sort waste, and every mahalla could organise a monthly haşar against plastic. When neighbours clean a canal together, they see the problem with their own eyes and are less likely to litter afterwards. In this way, new habits would spread from family to family.
Guard rail
Admittedly, neither solution is perfect. Fees may be unpopular at first, and volunteers may lose interest after a few months. To prevent this, the money from the fees could pay for recycling bins and a prize for the cleanest mahalla.
Right bank
In conclusion, plastic pollution is serious, but it is not hopeless. In my view, putting a price on plastic is the most effective first step, because it changes behaviour quickly. If we start today, our rivers will be cleaner tomorrow — so next time you go to the bazaar, take a cloth bag.

Be the examiner

Mark two paragraphs with the four criteria below. Then use the same criteria for your own essay.

CriterionA C1 essay …

Two students wrote Pillar 1 for the model-essay task (plastic waste in towns). Mark both.

Student A
Firstly, government must to ban the plastic bags in bazaars and shops. If government will ban bags, people will bring cloth bags from home, because they will have no other choice. For example, the shop in my mahalla already asks customers to bring their own bag, and now there is less litter in our street. This problem is very actual today. So we must solve this problem quickly.
Student B
A highly effective first step would be to put a price on single-use plastic. If shops charged even a small fee for every bag, many customers would simply bring their own. A case in point is the deposit schemes used in several European countries, where empty bottles are returned rather than dropped. Such a measure would go a long way towards keeping plastic off our streets.

Which criterion shows the biggest difference between A and B? Why?

Twelve words for planning a trip. Read the cards, say each word aloud and make a sentence.

itineraryNOUN a detailed plan of a journey: places, dates and timesSend me your itinerary.
accommodationNOUN a place to stay or live, e.g. a hotel roomcheap accommodation near the centre
enquireVERB · FORMAL ask someone officially for informationenquire about prices

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: Jasur from Kokand is planning a trip. Look at the two greetings. Who is each letter for? Tick the formal one.   “Hi Aziz,”   “Dear Sir or Madam,”

One Trip, Two Letters

An email and a letter written for this book: the people and the guesthouse are fictional · about 390 words · B2

EMAIL · To: Aziz · Subject: Road trip in May?!

Hi Aziz,

AHow are things in Tashkent? Sorry I haven’t written for ages — exams ate my whole life! Good news, though: I passed everything, so now I can finally think about the holidays. Kokand is very quiet without you, by the way.

BHere’s the plan. In the May holidays I want to do the big Silk Road trip: two days in Samarkand, then the train to Bukhara for three nights. I’ve already worked out a rough itinerary. Day one is the Registan, of course — I’ve wanted to see it at sunset since I was ten. In Bukhara I just want to get lost in the old city. On the last evening we could sit in a teahouse and plan our next trip — Khiva, maybe? I haven’t sorted out the train tickets yet, but I’ve found a small guesthouse that looks great.

CSo — fancy coming? It’ll be much more fun with you, and we can share the costs, so it won’t be expensive. You can take all the photos! Can you find out if your cousin in Bukhara can pick us up from the station? If not, I’ll ask the guesthouse. Let me know by Friday, OK?

Can’t wait!
Jasur

P.S. Bring your good camera, not just your phone.

LETTER · To: The Manager, Silk Road Guesthouse, Bukhara

Dear Sir or Madam,

DI am writing to enquire about accommodation at your guesthouse in May. I found your details on a travel website, and the reviews from previous guests were very positive.

EMy friend and I are university students, and we are planning to stay in Bukhara for three nights, from 5 to 8 May. I would be grateful if you could tell me whether a twin room is available on these dates. If possible, we would prefer a quiet room, as we will arrive after a long journey. Could you also let me know the price per night and whether breakfast is included?

FIn addition, I would like to know if you organise walking tours of the old city, as we are particularly interested in its history and architecture. If so, could you tell me how long the tours last? Finally, I would like to ask whether it is possible to arrange transport from the railway station.

GI would appreciate it if you could reply by 20 April, so that we can book our train tickets. Thank you in advance for your help. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Jasur Toshmatov

Find three differences in style between the email and the letter.
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on the email (A–C), Group B on paragraphs D–E, Group C on F–G. Read your part and list every question the writer asks. Then form new mixed groups and teach your part in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: Imagine Jasur sent paragraph C to the guesthouse manager. What would the manager think? Which letter was harder to write — and why?

Language toolkit: polite questions

10 MIN

Indirect questions make a request more polite. Use them in a formal letter.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in Jasur’s formal letter and complete them.

1. (E) I would be grateful if you tell me whether a twin room is available …

2. (E) Could you also let me know the price per night and breakfast is included?

3. (F) … I would like to know you organise walking tours of the old city …

4. (F) … could you tell me how long the tours ?

6. (G) I look forward to from you.

Direct → indirect rule
Direct questionPolite indirect questionWhat changes?
Is the room free?Could you tell me whether the room is free?add whether / if
How long do the tours last?Could you tell me how long the tours last?do goes
How much does a room cost?Could you let me know how much a room costs?does goes · costs
Can you send me a map?I would be grateful if you could send me a map.can → could

Three rules

  • Statement word order: where the station is ✓  ·  where is the station ✗
  • No do / does / did: if you organise tours ✓  ·  if do you organise tours ✗
  • End mark: Could you tell me … ends with ?  ·  I would like to know … ends with a full stop.

Broken sentenceFixed sentence

Level up: the C1 formal register

CONTINUED

At B2 your formal letter is correct. At C1 it is also smooth: requests sound gentle, ideas are packed into nouns, and the reader always knows which topic you are on.

ToolPhrasesExample
Softened requests
a request that leaves the reader free		I was wondering whether … · Would it be possible to …? · I would be most grateful if …I was wondering whether you could arrange transport from the station.
Formal inversion
“if” becomes Should		Should you require … · Should a deposit be necessary, …Should you require any further information, please do not hesitate to contact me.
Nominalisation
verb → noun		confirm → confirmation · arrive → arrival · pay → paymentCan I pay when I arrive? → Would payment on arrival be possible?
Topic signposts
tell the reader which topic is next		With regard to … · As regards … · Further to …With regard to the walking tour, could you tell me how long it lasts?

B2 sentenceC1 sentence

Do not over-soften

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: What do employers want to know about a young applicant? Tick two, then check in paragraph B.   your age   what you have done   your family   why you want the job

Your First Yes

A guide + one student’s letter · about 360 words · B2 · written for this book (fictional museum and people)

A“I can’t get a job without experience, and I can’t get experience without a job.” Many young people know this circle. Volunteering is one of the easiest ways to break it. Museums, festivals, sports events and charities often need extra hands, and they are usually happy to train beginners. A few weeks as a volunteer give you real experience, new skills and, often, a reference for your first paid job.

BBut first you have to win that place in writing. Most organisations ask for a short letter of application, and the person who reads it usually has many letters on the desk. A good letter answers three questions quickly: What have you done? What can you do? Why do you want this place? Keep it to one page, answer the advert and let your examples do the talking. Here is an advert from a museum in Margilan — and one student’s answer.

VOLUNTEER GUIDES WANTED
Silk Threads Museum, Margilan · June–August
We are looking for friendly students with good English to show international visitors around our weaving workshops. This is an unpaid position, but lunch and full training are provided. Please write to Ms Nodira Saidova, Volunteer Coordinator, by 15 May.

Dear Ms Saidova,

CI am writing to apply for the position of volunteer guide at the Silk Threads Museum, which I saw advertised on the museum’s website. I am a second-year student of English at a university in Fergana, and I would like to join your team this summer.

DI have volunteered at several events in the last two years. In 2025, I helped at a regional book fair, where I was responsible for welcoming guests. Last summer, I also worked in my aunt’s guesthouse, so I have already met many travellers from abroad.

EI speak Uzbek, Russian and English fluently. My friends describe me as reliable and well organised. I have also learnt to stay calm under pressure: at the book fair, I once looked after a group of forty schoolchildren on my own.

FI grew up in a family of weavers, and I have watched my grandmother make ikat fabric since I was a child. Being a guide would give me the chance to share this tradition with visitors and to improve my English.

GI am available from 1 June until the end of August, and I would be happy to attend an interview. I have attached my CV. Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours sincerely,
Dilnoza Karimova

Find the three questions from B in Dilnoza’s letter. Where is each answer?
Jigsaw option. Group A: the guide and the advert (A–B). Group B: C–D. Group C: E–G. What does your part tell the museum about Dilnoza? Teach it to a mixed group in 60 seconds.
Talk after reading: You are Ms Saidova. Would you invite Dilnoza to an interview? Which sentence in her letter is the strongest? Which would you change?

Language toolkit: have done or did?

10 MIN

Experience has two layers: the headline (present perfect) and the story (past simple).

Notice find it

Find these sentences in Dilnoza’s letter and complete them.

1. (D) I at several events in the last two years.

2. (D) In 2025, I at a regional book fair …

3. (D) Last summer, I also in my aunt’s guesthouse …

4. (D) … so I already many travellers from abroad.

5. (E) … at the book fair, I once after a group of forty schoolchildren …

6. (F) I my grandmother make ikat fabric since I was a child.

Headline and story rule
Present perfect · the headlinePast simple · the story
Formhave / has + past participlepast form (-ed or irregular)
Useexperience up to now · no finished timea detail at a finished time
Time wordsever · never · already · so far · in the last two years · since · forin 2025 · last summer · two years ago · when I was at school
ExampleI have worked with tourists.Last summer, I worked in a guesthouse.

Three rules

  • Finished time → past simple: In 2025 I organised … ✓  ·  In 2025 I have organised … ✗
  • Since / for → present perfect: I have studied English for six years ✓  ·  I study English for six years ✗
  • Headline first, then the story: I have volunteered at three events. Last May, I helped at …
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. I have worked at a summer camp last year.
2. I volunteer at the city library since 2024.
3. In 2025 I have organised a charity concert.
4. I have never be a guide before.
5. I study English for eight years.
☆Write about your experience write

One headline in the present perfect + two details in the past simple — about you.

Level up: presenting your experience

CONTINUED

At B2 you list what you have done. At C1 you package it: precise verbs, compact sentences and a confident but honest voice.

ToolPhrasesExample
Achievement verbs
say exactly what you did		coordinated · handled · supervised · ensured · set upAt the book fair, I handled enquiries from more than two hundred visitors.
Participle clauses
two facts in one sentence		Having worked as … , I … · Working with …, I learnt …Having volunteered at two festivals, I know how to stay calm in a crowd.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		speak well → a good command of · able → my ability to · experience inI speak English well. → I have a good command of English.
Confident hedging
sure, but not boastful		I believe I would be well suited to … · I am confident that … · I would welcome the opportunity to …I believe I would be well suited to this role, as I enjoy working with visitors.

The Blueprint: the letter of application

A letter of application is a key, and the job advert is the lock: every part of the letter must answer the advert. Its aim is an interview. Typical tasks: You saw this advert. Write a letter of application. · Apply for the position below.

Read the advert first: each tooth of your key must answer one of its requirements.

Part of the keyPart of the letterWhat goes insideWords
The bowOpeningthe position + where you saw it + who you are≈ 40
Tooth 1Experienceheadline (present perfect) + story (past simple)≈ 50
Tooth 2Skillslanguages, qualities — and proof≈ 40
Tooth 3Motivationwhy this job? why this organisation?≈ 40
The tipPolite closewhen you are available, CV, interview, thanks≈ 30
Compare it think
Formal letter (Stop 12)Letter of applicationA CV line
Goalget information or actionget an interviewlist facts fast
OpeningI am writing to enquire …I am writing to apply for …no greeting
Middledetails + polite questionsexperience, skills, motivationdates + facts
Styleformal, indirect questionsformal, confident, “I”notes, no “I”: 2025 · Volunteer, book fair
Buildingcarved gatekeythe label on the key

Model letter

CONTINUED
Advert: SUMMER RECEPTIONIST · Silk Road Guesthouse (fictional), Bukhara · June–August · Good English and a friendly smile essential. Write to Mr Rustam Nazarov, Manager. (Remember Jasur from Stop 12? He stayed there in May.)
Greeting
Dear Mr Nazarov,
The bow
POSITIONI am writing to apply for the position of summer receptionist, WHEREwhich I saw advertised on your website. WHOI am a second-year student of English from Kokand, and I would like to spend this summer gaining practical experience.
Tooth 1 · experience
(1) I have worked with visitors before. (2) Last summer, I helped at my uncle’s café in Kokand, where I took orders and looked after foreign guests. (3) In 2025, I also volunteered at a student conference and was responsible for registration.
Tooth 2 · skills
I speak Uzbek, Russian and English, and I can use booking apps and spreadsheets. I stay calm under pressure: at the conference, I registered more than a hundred participants in one morning. I am also punctual and well organised.
Tooth 3 · motivation
I stayed at your guesthouse last May and was impressed by how warmly your staff welcomed every guest. I would like to be part of a team like that and to learn how a small hotel works from the inside.
The tip
I am available from 10 June until 31 August and would be glad to attend an interview, online or in person. I have attached my CV. Thank you for considering my application. I look forward to hearing from you.
Sign-off
Yours sincerely,
Jasur Toshmatov

1. The bow: which job, and where did he see it?

2. Tooth 1: write PP (present perfect) or PS (past simple) for (1)–(3).

3. Tooth 2: what proves Jasur’s skill?

4. Tooth 3: why is this stronger than “I need money”?

5. Why Yours sincerely, not faithfully?

Jasur knows the manager’s name.
It is a letter about a job.
It sounds more friendly.

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: look at the title and the photo. What do you think the sea “did”? Tick one.
it froze in winter   it became much smaller   it moved to another country

The Sea That Walked Away

A student’s story · written for this book (Madina is fictional) · about 450 words · B2

AI had never wanted to go to Karakalpakstan. When our geography teacher announced a student trip to the Aral Sea region, I was reluctant. My friends were planning a week in the mountains, and a long train ride across the desert sounded like the most boring holiday possible. In the end, my mother made the decision for me. “You complain about everything,” she said. “Go and see something real.”

BWe set off from Tashkent on a cold April afternoon. All night, the train was rattling through the darkness while I was trying to sleep on a narrow top bunk. By the time the sun rose, the view had completely changed. A vast, flat desert stretched to the horizon, with only a few camels in sight. I pressed my face against the window. Nobody had told me that emptiness could be beautiful.

CAfter a night in Nukus, we boarded a small bus for Muynak. Our guide, a quiet man called Bakhtiyor, explained that Muynak had once been a busy fishing port. Families had lived from the sea for generations. I nodded politely, but I was not really listening. I was checking whether my phone had a signal.

DThen the bus broke down. We were driving along an empty road when the engine made a terrible noise and stopped. The driver shook his head and walked to the nearest village for help. We were stranded in the heat for three hours. At first, everyone complained. Then Bakhtiyor began to talk about his grandfather, who had caught fish in the Aral Sea when it was still blue and deep. As soon as he started, we all went quiet.

EWe reached Muynak late in the afternoon. As we walked along the old shore, I saw the ships. Rusty fishing boats were lying in the sand like sleeping animals, kilometres from any water. The wind was blowing dust into my eyes, and the only sound was a metal door banging somewhere. I stood next to a ship that had sailed on a real sea when my grandparents were young, and I felt completely overwhelmed.

FThat was my turning point. Before the trip, I had believed that environmental problems happened far away, in other countries or on TV. Now I knew that a whole sea could shrink in one lifetime, in my own country, because of decisions people had made.

GI came home exhausted, sunburnt and quiet. My mother asked if it had been boring. “No,” I said. “It was the most important week of my life.” Since then, I have joined a student eco-club, and I tell everyone about Muynak. Some journeys take you somewhere new. The best ones change who you are.

Where does the story stop moving fast and slow down? Why there?
Jigsaw option. Group A becomes the expert on paragraphs A–B (departure), Group B on C–D (the obstacle), Group C on E–F (the turning point). Read your part, agree what happens and how the writer feels, then form mixed groups and retell it in 60 seconds. Read G together.
Talk after reading: Which moment in the story could you see most clearly? Which words helped you see it?

Language toolkit: narrative tenses

10 MIN

A story has three clocks: what happened next, what was going on, and what had happened before.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the story and complete them.

1. (B) All night, the train through the darkness while I to sleep.

2. (B) By the time the sun rose, the view completely .

3. (D) We along an empty road when the engine a terrible noise.

4. (D) As soon as he , we all went quiet.

5. (A) I to go to Karakalpakstan.

6. (E) I stood next to a ship that on a real sea …

Three narrative tenses rule
TenseFormJob in the storyExample from the story
Past simplewent · sawmain events in orderWe reached Muynak.
Past continuouswas / were + -ingbackground actionThe wind was blowing.
Past perfecthad + past participlea jump back in timeMuynak had once been a port.

Time linkers

  • while + a long action: While I was trying to sleep, the train was rattling.
  • when + a short action that interrupts: We were driving when the engine stopped.
  • as soon as = immediately after · by the time + past simple → past perfect in the other half
  • In the end = finally ✓  ·  at the end of something (the road, the day) ✓
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. While I walked to the station, it was starting to rain.
2. When we arrived, the bus already left.
3. By the time we reached Nukus, I have read my book.
4. Suddenly I was knowing the answer.
5. As soon as I was seeing the ships, I stopped.

Level up: C1 narrative tools

At B2 your story moves in the right order. At C1 you control it: smooth actions, a spotlight on the key moment and an honest look back.

ToolPhrasesExample
Participle clauses
two actions in one		Pressing …, I … · Having waited …, we … · Exhausted, I …Having waited three hours in the heat, we finally heard the engine start.
Inversion
stop at the key moment		Little did I know that … · No sooner had … than … · Never had I …Little did I know that this trip would change my plans for university.
Cleft sentences
spotlight one moment		It was only when … that … · What I remember most is …It was only when I touched the rusty hull that I understood.
Reflective stance
look back		Looking back, … · In hindsight, … · Ironically, … · It was then that …Ironically, the trip I had refused to take became the one I talk about most.

The Blueprint: the narrative essay

10 MIN

A narrative essay tells a true (or true-to-life) story in time order and shows what it meant to you. Typical tasks: Write about a time when … · Describe a journey that changed you · Tell the story of …

A narrative needs an obstacle. Slow down at the turning point and end with what you learned.

Stage of the routePart of the essayWhat goes insideWords
1 · DepartureParagraph 1Hook → who, where, when, why → a hint of your mood≈ 50
2 · The obstacleParagraph 2Something goes wrong: a problem or conflict; tension rises≈ 70
3 · Turning pointParagraph 3The climax: slow down, use the senses, show the feeling≈ 70
4 · ArrivalConclusionHow it ended + what I learned / how I changed≈ 50
Compare it think
Narrative (Stop 14)Opinion (Stop 8)Problem–solution (Stop 11)
Goaltake the reader on your journeywin the reader to one sidefix a problem, step by step
Ordertime: first → then → in the endreason 1 → reason 2problem → solutions
Tensespast simple, continuous, perfectmostly presentpresent + conditionals
Buildingcaravan route mapmadrasabridge

Model essay

CONTINUED
Task: Write a narrative essay about a journey that changed the way you see something.
Departure
HOOKI was seventeen, and I had never travelled anywhere without my parents. SCENEOne hot August morning, I took the early train from Bukhara to Khiva, where my older cousin was waiting for me. MOODI had a small bag, a new phone and far too much confidence. For the first two hours, I watched the desert through the dusty window and felt very grown-up.
The obstacle
The trouble started (1) at a small station in the desert. While I was buying (2) water on the platform, the doors closed (3). The train moved. I ran. It was too late. My bag was still inside. I stood there in the heat with a bottle of water and a phone with two per cent battery. By the time I understood what had happened, the train had disappeared (4).
Turning point
Then an old woman, who had been selling melons in the shade of the station wall, came slowly over to me. She did not ask many questions; instead, she called her grandson, who had a car, and while we were waiting, she cut a slice of melon and put it into my hand. I still remember its sweetness, the smell of hot dust and her calm voice: “It’s nothing, my child. Everyone gets lost once.”
Arrival
An hour later, her grandson drove me to the next station, where the station master was keeping my bag. I reached Khiva that evening, tired but safe, and my cousin laughed at my story all through dinner. Looking back, that journey taught me that strangers are often kinder than we expect. Since then, whenever I see a lost traveller, I stop and help.

1. Departure: find the scene.

Who? When?

Where?

2. Obstacle: write PS (past simple), PC (past continuous) or PP (past perfect).

☆3. Turning point: find three details for the senses.

4. Arrival: what did the writer learn? How do we know the writer really changed?

5. The story ends with …

a question to the reader
a lesson + a change in behaviour
a prediction about the future

6. Speed check: the obstacle has short, quick sentences; the turning point has longer, slower ones. Why?

☆7. This model is B2+. Upgrade two of its sentences with the Level-up tools.

Flat story → Vivid story

8 MIN

A flat sentence tells. A vivid sentence shows. Rewrite each flat sentence: add a specific detail, a strong verb and at least one sense — sight, sound, smell, touch or taste.

FLAT · tellsThe train was crowded and I was tired.
→
Every bunk was taken, a baby was crying two seats away, and my eyes kept closing against the cold window.
FLAT · tellsThe desert was beautiful.
→
FLAT · tellsI was scared when the bus stopped.
→
FLAT · tellsWe arrived and I was happy.
→

Tool tips: specific nouns (not “food” but “hot somsa”) · strong verbs (rattled, banged, whispered) · show the feeling through the body (my hands were shaking) · one sense per sentence is enough

Phrase bank use these
JobB2 · safeC1 · upgrade
Set the sceneI will never forget the day … · It was a cold morning in …It was the kind of morning when … · Never had I felt so … as on the day …
Move the storyAt first, … · Then … · As soon as …, … · By the time …, …No sooner had … than … · Having …, I …
Build tensionSuddenly, … · To make matters worse, …Without warning, … · Little did I know that …
Reach the turning pointThat was the moment when … · I realised that …It was only when … that I … · For the first time, it dawned on me that …
Arrive and reflectIn the end, … · That journey taught me … · Since then, I have …Looking back, … · In hindsight, … · Ironically, …

Common traps

✗ Yesterday I go to the station and I see Jasur.
✓ Yesterday I went to the station and saw Jasur.
✗ The trip was long and I was very boring.
✓ The trip was long and I was very bored.
✗ When we arrived, the train already left.
✓ When we arrived, the train had already left.
✗ At the end, I understood everything.
✓ In the end, I understood everything.

Words for the five senses

Sight · dusty, glittering, pale, a rusty hull, the last light
Sound · rattling, banging, whispering, total silence
Smell · smoke, ripe melons, hot dust, fresh bread
Touch · burning sand, a cold window, a rough rope
Taste · salty air, sweet tea, warm somsa
Body · shaking hands, a dry throat, heavy eyes

3

Read like a detective

17 MIN

Before you read: the article is about sport. What else? Tick one.   food   writing   money

Move More, Think Better

A magazine article · about 430 words · B2 · written for this book

AFor many students, a typical day looks like this: an hour on a bus, six hours in a lecture hall and an evening in front of a laptop. By the end of the week, the only exercise some of them get is climbing the stairs to the third floor. This sedentary lifestyle has become so normal that we rarely notice it. Our bodies, however, do notice.

BThe human body is designed to move. When we exercise regularly, the heart becomes stronger, the lungs work more efficiently and the muscles stay healthy. Doctors agree that physical activity lowers the risk of many serious illnesses, including heart disease and type 2 diabetes. The World Health Organization recommends that adults do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity every week, which is a little over twenty minutes a day.

CSport is not only good for the body; it also helps the mind. Exercise can boost your mood, reduce stress and help you sleep better. Many students find that a short walk between study sessions clears their head. A student who has been sitting still for hours often thinks more clearly after ten minutes of movement than after another cup of coffee.

DOf course, nobody becomes an athlete overnight. One of the most common mistakes that beginners make is doing too much too soon. A person who has not run for years and suddenly runs ten kilometres may suffer an injury and give up. Coaches usually advise starting with moderate exercise, warming up properly and building up stamina step by step.

EIn Uzbekistan, there is no shortage of ways to stay active. Football is played in mahallas all over the country, and kuraş, the traditional Uzbek wrestling, is taught in many sports schools. Early in the morning, parks in Tashkent are full of people who walk, jog or exercise together. Nobody needs expensive equipment to take up a sport: a pair of trainers and a friend are usually enough.

FInterestingly, the way athletes improve has a lesson for students. A good coach watches a training session, points out what went well and suggests one or two things to change. The athlete tries again, and the next performance is a little better. Nobody expects a perfect result on the first attempt. Progress is a cycle: try, get feedback, try again.

GThe same cycle works in writing. A first draft is like a first training session: it shows where you are, not where you could be. So close the laptop for a while, go for a walk with a friend — and then come back and make your work better.

Look at F and G. What does a coach have in common with a good editor?
Jigsaw option. Group A: paragraphs A–C · Group B: D–E · Group C: F–G. Become experts on your part, then teach it to a new mixed group in 60 seconds. Read paragraph F twice: it is this whole lesson in five sentences.
Talk after reading: Which piece of advice in the article will you actually try this week? Which one is hard for you? Why?

Language toolkit: agreement and articles

10 MIN

Two small things cause most red marks in student essays: verb agreement and a / an / the.

Notice find it

Find these sentences in the article and complete them.

1. (B) The human body designed to move.

2. (D) One of the most common mistakes that beginners make doing too much too soon.

3. (E) Nobody expensive equipment to take up a sport …

4. (E) … a pair of trainers and a friend usually enough.

5. (B) World Health Organization recommends that adults …

6. (C) Many students find that short walk between study sessions clears their head.

The rules rule
RuleExample from the article
He / she / it / one thing → verb + -sExercise boosts your mood. · The athlete tries again.
Find the head noun (not the nearest)One of the most common mistakes … is …
Nobody / every … → singularNobody needs expensive equipment.
a / an → one of many, first mentionStudents find that a short walk clears their head.
the → the only one / we know whichthe heart · the World Health Organization
no article → things in generalSport is not only good for the body …

Three rules

  • Uncountable = singular: Regular exercise is … · Health is … · Advice helps …
  • Sport, health, nature in general: no the: The health is important ✗ → Health is important ✓
  • A singular countable noun needs an article: He is student ✗ → He is a student ✓
Fix it correct
Broken sentenceFixed sentence
1. Regular exercise make you stronger.
2. The number of students who do sport are growing.
3. My brother is student and he plays the football.
4. Everyone in my group want to join the gym.
5. The health is more important than money.

Level up: redraft to C1

CONTINUED

Fixing errors makes a draft correct. Four editing moves make it C1: sharper words, ideas packed into nouns, sentences that point back to each other and recommendations that sound careful, not bossy.

ToolPhrasesExample
Precise vocabulary
replace vague words		good → beneficial · bad → detrimental · do → introduce / provide · a lot → a great dealSport is good for students. → Regular exercise is highly beneficial for students.
Nominalisation
verb or adjective → noun		reduce → a reduction in · lack · the introduction of · participation inThe introduction of free sports clubs would increase participation in sport.
Cohesive reference
point back to an idea		This approach … · Such measures … · This lack of …Many students never exercise. This lack of activity affects their grades.
Hedged recommendations
careful, not bossy		could consider … · it would be advisable to … · one option would be to …Universities could consider opening their sports halls in the evening.

B2 sentenceC1 sentence

Remember from Stop 8: do not over-hedge

✗ Universities could perhaps possibly consider maybe opening some gyms.
✓ Universities could consider opening free gyms.  — one hedge per recommendation is enough.

The Blueprint: draft, feedback, redraft

10 MIN

A koşinkor (tile-maker) never sells the first tile. He shapes the clay, a master marks it, he fixes it — then he glazes and fires it. Process writing works the same way: draft → feedback → redraft.

A redraft improves the same text: keep what works and change what the feedback shows.

In the workshopIn writingWhat you doWho
Raw clayFirst draftGet your ideas down fast. Follow your hovli plan. Don’t stop to fix spelling.you
Marked tilePeer feedbackA partner reads, gives two stars and a wish and marks grammar with symbols.partner
Second firingRedraftAct on the wish: add an example, cut a weak sentence, move ideas, fix errors.you
GlazeProofreadLast check: agreement, articles, spelling, punctuation. Read it aloud.you
Compare it think
First draftRedraftProofread
Focusideasstructure and claritysmall errors
QuestionWhat do I want to say?Will the reader understand?Is every word correct?
Tileraw claymarked and reshapedglazed and shining

Model: draft, feedback, redraft

CONTINUED
Task: How can universities help students to lead a healthier life? Jasur wrote Room 1 of his essay. Dilnoza was his editor. (Fictional students; the texts were written for this book.)
Draft
raw clay
Firstly, universities should open sport clubs. The most of students sits all day in lectures, and they has no time for sport. Sport help us to stay healthy, and it is also good for mind. For example the football. So universities must do it.
Feedback
marks
★ I really liked your topic sentence: it answers the question clearly.
★ Good point that sport helps the mind, not only the body.
✦ Wish: It might be clearer if you gave a real example instead of “the football”. What could a club actually do? Also, “do it” is vague — you could end by linking back to students’ health.
Grammar detective: 3 × agreement (A) · 3 × articles (Art)
Redraft
glazed tile
(1) Firstly, universities should open free sport clubs for their students. (2) Most students sit in lectures all day, and many of them have no time for sport in the evening. (3) Regular exercise helps us to stay healthy, and it is also good for the mind, because it reduces stress before exams. (4) For example, a university football or volleyball club could train twice a week after classes. (5) In this way, universities could protect both their students’ health and their grades.

Errors: a busy people → busy people · It do not → It does not · a special equipment → special equipment · My grandmother walk → walks · she feel → feels.

Student A: T 2 · O 2 · V 2 · G 1 (a relevant measure with a reason and a personal example, but must to build sounds bossy; point → reason → example → window, but the window is vague; free gym, costs a lot, but very important; many agreement and article errors: the universities, The most of students has, sport club, my friend go, So gym is). Student B: T 3 · O 3 · V 3 · G 3. The biggest difference is in G (2 points).
